solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Impression made by Napoleon in the field?

definitions.text: Impression made by Napoleon in the field?

parts.note: the surface pushes the emperor making an impression on history, or an impersonation of him
meant literally: Napoleon the pig of Animal Farm, pressing a print into a farm field

explanation.surface: The emperor leaves his mark on a battlefield.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface summons the French emperor and a battlefield; this Napoleon is the pig who runs Orwell's Animal Farm, and his impression in a field is a print left by a trotter.
explanation.definitionFit: A cryptic definition: an impression is a print in soft ground, and a pig on a farm leaves one with each step.

clue.text: Exhibit artist mounted for BA workshop?

indicators.note: to mount is to climb, and in a down clue climbing makes the letters read bottom to top

parts.note: to hang pictures is to exhibit them
RA, a Royal Academician, climbs the column

explanation.surface: A gallery hangs an artist's work for a university arts workshop.
explanation.walkthrough: BA looks like the Bachelor of Arts degree that suits the gallery picture; it is British Airways, whose workshop is where planes are kept and repaired.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example with a question mark: an airline such as BA services its planes in a hangar, so it is that airline's workshop.

clue.text: Take place of wretch bolstering bare rock

indicators.note: something bare has had its covering taken off, so the rock loses its outer letters
a bolster props something up, so in a down clue the wretch sits beneath the rock

parts.note: ROCK with its outer letters stripped
a cur is a contemptible wretch

explanation.surface: A miserable soul supports himself on a bare rock in the wilderness.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Take place of' wants to mean 'replace'; the definition stops at 'Take place', and 'of' only links it to the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: things that occur happen, or take place.

clue.text: American topless in tiny bathing suit

indicators.note: without a top, so the word loses its first letter
the shortened American is put inside the next word

parts.note: mini = tiny; it holds the American
YANK, an American, loses its top letter

explanation.surface: A topless American strolls a beach in a skimpy swimsuit.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface pictures a topless beachgoer, which suits the answer: a mankini is a man's sling-style swimsuit, notorious from the film Borat.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by class: the mankini is one kind of bathing suit, a very skimpy one for men.

clue.text: After depression it gets you hopping from the chair

definitions.text: After depression it gets you hopping from the chair

parts.words: After depression it gets you hopping
parts.note: the surface pushes a lifted mood that has you jumping up; depression is really a pressed button, and hopping is channel-hopping
you never leave the seat: the hopping is done from the armchair

explanation.surface: Someone sinks into gloom and then leaps out of their armchair.
explanation.walkthrough: Depression and hopping suggest a mood and a jump; the depression is a pressed button, and the hopping is channel-hopping without leaving your seat.
explanation.definitionFit: A cryptic definition: pressing the remote's button is a depression, and it lets a viewer hop channels without rising from the armchair.

clue.text: Plant plants killing time in vacated area

indicators.note: to kill something is to do away with it, so time, T, is removed
the shortened plants go inside the area
a vacated space has been emptied, so the word keeps only its outer letters

parts.note: AREA emptied of its middle; it holds the plants
CACTI without T for time

explanation.surface: A gardener's instruction to plant things and kill time in an empty patch.
explanation.walkthrough: The first 'Plant' is the definition, a noun; the second word, 'plants', is wordplay, and the verb reading of both is the misdirection.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by class: the acacia, or wattle, is a tree or shrub and so a plant.

clue.text: Lug wax from odd space below church

indicators.note: in a down clue, what is below comes later, so the odd space follows the church

parts.note: Church of England
rum = odd, strange
an en is a printer's space

explanation.surface: Wax taken from a strange space beneath a church, as if in a crypt.
explanation.walkthrough: Lug is the Scots and northern English word for ear, so lug wax is earwax; the church and its crypt are just scenery.
explanation.definitionFit: A regional use: lug is dialect for ear, and cerumen is the medical name for earwax.

clue.text: Noisy fool leaves lesson in love

indicators.note: the fool departs from the lesson, taking its letters with it

parts.note: CLASS, a lesson, loses ASS, a fool
amorous = in love

explanation.surface: A loud idiot walks out of a class about romance.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lesson in love' reads as one phrase; the split falls after 'lesson', so 'in love' is its own piece.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a clamorous crowd is loud and shouting, or noisy.

clue.text: Warm Sea periodically laps second egg fossil

indicators.note: at regular intervals, so every other letter is taken
water laps round a shore, so these letters wrap round the next pieces

parts.note: the even letters of WARM SEA; they wrap the rest
a mo is a moment, a second
a nit is a louse's egg

explanation.surface: A warm sea laps over a fossilised egg on the shore.
explanation.walkthrough: The seaside scene is apt, since ammonites are the classic beach fossil; the capital on Sea is there only to dress the phrase up.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by class: the ammonite is a coiled shell of an extinct mollusc, one of the commonest fossils.

clue.text: Stevie perhaps bored by nasty mean barbs?

indicators.note: the letters of mean are treated badly and come out in a new order
to be bored by something is to have it drilled into you, so the surname holds the rearranged letters

parts.note: Stevie Nicks, singer with Fleetwood Mac; her surname holds the rest
MEAN rearranged

explanation.surface: The singer Stevie is wounded by spiteful jibes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stevie perhaps' looks like the definition, a pet form of Steven; it is Stevie Nicks, and the barbs themselves are the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example with a question mark: taunting nicknames are verbal barbs aimed at someone.

clue.text: Circles 'misfit' sadly in judgement of one's worth

indicators.note: things that have gone sadly are in a sorry state, so the letters are in disorder

parts.note: anagram fodder, 13 letters

explanation.surface: Social circles unkindly label someone a misfit, as a verdict on their worth.
explanation.walkthrough: The quotation marks make 'misfit' look like a label pinned on someone, which fits the answer's mood nicely.
explanation.definitionFit: A paraphrase: self-criticism is you judging yourself, a verdict on your own worth.

clue.text: Brazilian capital essentially dynamises province

parts.note: the real is Brazil's currency

indicators.note: the essence of a thing is its core, so the central letter is taken

parts.note: the middle letter of DYNAMISES

explanation.surface: Brasília, the capital, energises its surrounding state.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Brazilian capital' wants to be the city Brasília; it is capital as money, the real.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym in the figurative sense: one's province or realm is one's field of activity or domain.

clue.text: Best flirt organised rescue if all routes blocked?

indicators.note: to organise is to put in order, so the letters of flirt are arranged afresh

parts.note: A1 = first-rate, with the 1 written as I
FLIRT rearranged

explanation.surface: A top flirt arranges a rescue when every road is closed.
explanation.walkthrough: When roads are blocked, supplies or people are flown out: the definition is a whole scenario, hence the question mark.
explanation.definitionFit: A descriptive definition: when every road is cut, the way to rescue people is to fly them out.

clue.text: Charlie installing electrical unit in satire

indicators.note: to install something is to fit it inside, so the unit goes within the fool

parts.note: a charlie is a fool, a loon; it holds the unit
amp, the unit of current

explanation.surface: An electrician called Charlie fits a unit, as a scene in a comedy sketch.
explanation.walkthrough: Charlie looks like a name or the letter C; in British slang a charlie is a fool.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a lampoon is a satirical attack, so it is a piece of satire.

clue.text: Queen's beloved pop icon meets with Italian group

indicators.note: names the language, so 'with' is to be translated into Italian

parts.note: Prince, the American pop star
con = with in Italian
a sort is a group or kind

explanation.surface: A pop star meets an Italian band, with a nod to the band Queen.
explanation.walkthrough: Queen and pop icon pull toward the rock band; the title is the husband of a reigning queen, such as Prince Albert.
explanation.definitionFit: A descriptive definition: a prince consort is the husband of a reigning queen, so her beloved.

clue.text: Theft of extremely fine cloth hidden by mansion?

indicators.note: what is hidden by something is covered by it, so the mansion wraps round these letters

parts.note: a pile is a stately home; it holds the rest

indicators.note: at the extremes, so only the first and last letters are taken

parts.note: outer letters of FINE
a rag is a piece of cloth

explanation.surface: Fine fabric is stolen and stashed away in a country house.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Theft of extremely fine cloth' reads as one crime; 'of' is only the link, and the fine cloth is wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: pilferage is petty stealing, so a kind of theft.

clue.text: Sensitive way to stop Mickey's horde cycling?

indicators.note: a cycle goes round, so the last letter wheels round to the front
a stopper plugs a gap, so the way sits inside

parts.note: Mickey is a mouse, so his horde is MICE; cycled, the final letter moves to the front
a path is a way

explanation.surface: A gentle way to halt Mickey Mouse's rampaging kin as they pedal about.
explanation.walkthrough: Cycling looks like the mice are on bicycles; it is a letter rotation.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: an empathic person is sensitive to what others feel.

clue.text: Factories circling island anger small flush person

indicators.note: to circle something is to go round it, so the factories surround the next pieces

parts.note: mills = factories; they circle the island and anger
Iona, an island off western Scotland
ire = anger
s = small, as on clothing labels

explanation.surface: Mill-owners enrage an island's small, red-faced resident.
explanation.walkthrough: Flush looks like a blush or a toilet; here it means rich, with money to spare.
explanation.definitionFit: A slang sense: flush means well supplied with money, and a millionairess is a very rich woman.

clue.text: Parisian's here with head cold that's severe

indicators.note: a Parisian speaks French, so 'here' is to be given in French

parts.note: ici = here in French
a ness is a headland

explanation.surface: A Parisian arrives with a head cold that has become serious.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Head cold' reads as one illness; the split falls between them, with head as the headland and cold starting the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A paraphrase: iciness is cold severe enough to freeze.

clue.text: Fabric hoisted across tops of the hips isn't proper

indicators.note: hoisting lifts something, and in a down clue lifted letters read bottom to top
the top of a word is its first letter, so each word gives its initial

parts.note: LACE, a fabric, raised up the column; it holds the tops

indicators.note: stretched across something, so the fabric spans over the next letters

parts.note: first letters of THE HIPS ISN’T

explanation.surface: Lace pulled up over the hips is judged indecent.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is a dress-code complaint, which sits neatly beside an answer meaning proper.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym in the moral sense: ethical conduct is right and proper.

clue.text: Most of English town ultimately felt dated

indicators.note: most but not all of the word, so its last letter is dropped

parts.note: OLDHAM, a town near Manchester, without its last letter

indicators.note: in the end, so the word gives its final letter

parts.note: last letter of FELT

explanation.surface: Much of an English town feels behind the times.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Felt' sits by 'dated' as if both were verbs of feeling; felt is only the source of a final T.
explanation.definitionFit: An idiom: something old hat is so familiar it is out of date.

clue.text: Studio had story right

parts.note: had a meal = ate
a story is a fib, a lie
r = right

explanation.surface: A film studio owns the rights to a story.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Had story right' reads as owning a story's rights; each word is a separate piece.
explanation.definitionFit: A borrowing from French: atelier is the French word for a workshop, used in English for an artist's studio.

clue.text: Dubious naked maiden by meadow recalled prophet

indicators.note: something naked has had its covering taken off, so the word loses its outer letters
to recall is to call back, so the meadow is read backwards

parts.note: FISHY, dubious, stripped of its first and last letters
m = maiden, a maiden over in cricket scoring
LEA, a meadow, turned round

explanation.surface: A doubtful naked girl by a meadow remembers a prophet.
explanation.walkthrough: Ishmael, son of Abraham, is honoured as a prophet in Islam.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: Ishmael is revered as a prophet in the Islamic tradition.

clue.text: Solitary marine creature abandoned by sailor

indicators.note: deserted by the sailor, who leaves and takes his letters with him

parts.note: the abalone, a sea snail
AB, able seaman; these letters go

explanation.surface: A lonely sea creature deserted by a seaman.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is the answer in miniature: the creature is left on its own.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: to be solitary is to be on your own, with no company.

clue.text: Paradise for the large part is swell

indicators.note: for the most part but not all, so the word loses its last letter

parts.note: paradise is the afterlife above; drop its final N

explanation.surface: Paradise, for the most part, is wonderful.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Swell' reads as the adjective, great; it is the verb, to rise and heave like the sea.
explanation.definitionFit: A verb sense: the sea or a chest heaves when it rises and swells.

clue.text: Garment left poor Colin hot

indicators.note: in a poor state, so the letters are damaged and come out in a new order

parts.note: l = left
COLIN HOT rearranged

explanation.surface: Poor sweltering Colin has left his clothes behind.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface has Colin too hot to stay dressed, which is exactly the answer: the least clothing possible.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by class: the loincloth is a simple wrap round the hips, a garment at its most minimal.

clue.text: Musical replacing opening with another key line

indicators.note: the opening is the first letter, and it is replaced by the new one

parts.note: Grease, the musical
C, a musical key, replaces G, another key

explanation.surface: A musical shifts into a different key for its closing line.
explanation.walkthrough: G and C are both keys, so the swap is one key for another; line reads as a lyric but is a fold mark.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a crease is a line pressed into cloth or paper by folding.

clue.text: Most tiny powerless lights put back in case

indicators.note: without power, so P, the physics symbol for power, is removed
put back to front, so the letters are read in reverse

parts.note: LAMPS without P, turned round
lest = in case

explanation.surface: Tiny dead bulbs are put back in their box.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In case' looks like a container instruction; it is the word lest.
explanation.definitionFit: A superlative paraphrase: smallest is small at its most, tiny as can be.
